name: Firezone
license: Apache 2.0 for the clients, Gateway and Relay; Elastic License 2.0 for the Elixir admin portal and control plane
summary: Zero-trust access over WireGuard: a hosted control plane decides who may reach each private host, subnet or DNS name, and Gateways you run inside the network connect out to approved clients.
intro: Firezone has three parts. You run Gateways, small Rust binaries with no persistent storage, inside each private network (a Site), as Docker containers or systemd services. Users install the Firezone Client on Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS or Android, or run a headless client on servers, which can sign in with a service-account token. Firezone runs the rest as SaaS: the admin portal, the control plane API and the policy engine, written in Elixir and Phoenix and hosted on Azure, plus STUN/TURN relays in several regions. You define Resources (an IP, a CIDR range, or a DNS name such as `*.corp.example.com`) and Policies that say which identity-provider group may reach which Resource. Access is denied unless a Policy allows it.

Traffic doesn’t pass through a central VPN server. The client contains a small DNS resolver: when an app looks up a protected name, it gets a placeholder address, and the first packet to it triggers a request to the policy engine. If a Policy allows it, the control plane hands WireGuard keys to the client and to a nearby Gateway, and the two punch through NAT to talk directly, falling back to a relay that can’t decrypt the traffic. Gateways and clients only open outbound connections, so no inbound firewall ports are needed, and session keys rotate every two minutes. Since August 2026 the connection checks also travel inside WireGuard, so an observer sees nothing on the wire but WireGuard packets.

The code is on GitHub: the data plane is Apache 2.0 and the portal is under the Elastic License 2.0. Self-hosting is allowed but production self-hosting is not supported, and published clients are only guaranteed to work with the managed service. Plans in October 2026: Starter is free for up to 6 users, Team is $5 per user a month, Business is $8 per user a month and adds directory sync with Google, Entra ID and Okta, device posture checks and log sinks, and Enterprise is custom. A REST API, a Terraform provider and a CLI arrived in 2026.
strengths: Users get access to specific hosts, subnets or DNS names rather than a whole network, decided per Resource by group-based Policies
Direct, end-to-end encrypted WireGuard connections between client and Gateway, with relays only as a fallback, so there is no central VPN concentrator to size
No inbound ports: Gateways dial out, and stateful cloud firewalls (security groups, NSGs, GCP rules) need no changes
Gateways are stateless and configured by one token; running several per Site gives high availability, and capacity grows by adding more
limits: The control plane is Firezone’s SaaS: production self-hosting isn’t supported, so sign-in and policy changes depend on Firezone’s service
Not entirely open source: the portal and control plane are under the Elastic License 2.0, not an OSI licence
Directory sync, device posture checks and log sinks need the Business plan or higher, and Business caps an account at 1,000 users and 200 Sites
It works at layer 3, deciding which addresses a device can reach; it doesn’t record sessions or hand out per-session credentials the way identity-aware proxies such as Boundary do

# Outbound only: HTTPS 443 to the control plane, UDP to relays and clients. No inbound ports.

story: Jamil Bou Kheir, a former Cisco engineer, wanted an easy way to deploy and manage a WireGuard VPN. WireGuard supplies the tunnel but leaves key distribution, user management and routing tables to you, which he called “tedious and error-prone”. He left his job and built Firezone in Elixir and Phoenix: a self-hosted WireGuard VPN server with a web UI. It launched on Hacker News in 2021, was backed by Y Combinator, and by mid-2023 had more than 3,000 known running instances.

In July 2023 he announced Firezone 1.0, “an entirely new product with a brand new architecture”. A perimeter VPN trusts everyone once they are inside, so one stolen credential can expose the whole network. Firezone 1.0 instead brokers access to each resource: the protected side sits behind its firewall, keeps an outbound control channel to Firezone, and connects out to a client only after a policy allows it. The control plane became a hosted service with native clients for every platform.

Firezone 0.7, renamed Firezone Legacy, stopped getting updates after 31 January 2024, and 1.0 became generally available on 1 April 2024 with a $5-per-user Team plan. In 2026 the company shipped a redesigned portal, a REST API, a Terraform provider, a CLI and a Business plan, and removed ICE from the data path so that only WireGuard packets appear on the wire.

choices.why: WireGuard is a small, fast, well-reviewed tunnel protocol in every major OS. What it lacks is key distribution, user management and routing, which is exactly what Firezone adds.

choices.choice: Broker access per resource instead of running a VPN server
choices.why: A perimeter VPN grants the whole network after one login. Letting a policy engine approve each resource, and having the protected side connect outward, removes both broad access and open inbound ports.

choices.choice: A hosted control plane, open data plane
choices.why: Running the portal as a service let a small team ship native clients, high availability and fast policy updates; the Rust clients, Gateway and relay stay Apache 2.0 so the parts that touch your traffic can be inspected.

choices.choice: Keep control-plane and data-plane state apart
choices.why: Packet processing should never wait on a control message, and existing connections should survive a control-plane outage.
